attribution_limitations: The start of tofacitinib is dated October 30, 2019 (day 1) in the text and the Figure 1 caption, while the Table 1 caption and the text introducing the table label the November 1 column as initiation of tofacitinib. Nintedanib is dated November 18 (day 20) consistently.
The text places the highest measured ferritin of 1973 μg/L before the decision to start tofacitinib on October 30, 2019, while Table 1 prints 1973 in the November 1 column.
The text says serum ferritin rose from 428 to 1,695 μg/L with the pulmonary complication, while Table 1 prints 1,468 μg/L in the October 21 (admission) column and 428 on October 1, 2019.

Text-numbered days and table dates differ slightly: the text gives day 132 as March 9, 2020 (ferritin 304 μg/L, last visit) whereas Table 1 labels the last column March 8, 2020 (ferritin 304) and 18 weeks after starting tofacitinib; the text gives ferritin 717 μg/L on day 50 while the table gives 722 on December 25.

In the Flow cytometry row of Table 1, the dates October 23 and October 30 are printed under the October 21 (admission) and November 1 columns, and the footnote says flow cytometry was done on the same dates except for October 23 and 30, 2019. The Figure 3 caption dates the CD4 count of 264 cells/µl to October 23, the second day of admission.

The CD4/CD8 row label prints the unit /µl although the values (3.8 to 7.0) are ratios, and the text calls the ratio raised at 4.6 at the end of the reported period (table value 4.6 for March 8, 2020).

The text says the NK cell deficiency was first detected when the patient presented, while the abstract and discussion describe the five-month course; the Figure 3 caption words the recovery as normal levels (106 cells/µl) at the end of the observation period and the table prints 106 for March 8, 2020.

The abstract says correction of hyperferritinemia occurred with tofacitinib, but the last ferritin values (304 μg/L) are printed beside a reference range of 13–150 μg/L; the source does not state whether ferritin normalized.
The text says lung transplantation was discussed ("whether she should be considered"); it does not say transplantation was planned or performed.

The discussion attributes the shift from anti-Mi-2 detected in 2011 to anti-Jo-1 to "epitope spreading" as a best explanation and hypothesizes NK cell redistribution to the lung; these are the authors’ interpretations, and the Mi-2 test in 2011 was in an outside laboratory while the 2019 panel reports Mi-2 negative.

The admission is dated October 21, 2019, while the Figure 1 caption places the October 22, 2019 CT "on hospital admission" and the Figure 3 caption calls October 23 the second day of admission; the day count does not match the stated admission date exactly.

Figure 3B is described as a representative example of flow cytometry histograms; the caption does not state the date of the sample, and the near absence of NK cells is a caption statement about that example.

caption_claims.text: FIGURE 2 Timeline of pharmacologic interventions, changes in serum ferritin levels and FVC from October 2019 until March 2020. While the patient was treated with high-dose prednisone, azathioprine and tacrolimus ①, the respiratory function suddenly deteriorated and serum ferritin levels (y-axis left) rose from 428 to 1,695 μg/L (reference range 13–150 μg/L, dashed line). Pulse therapy with methylprednisolone and IVIG ② were followed by an ephemeral decrease in serum ferritin levels, which rebounded to the maximum measured value of 1973 μg/L. With the administration of tofacitinib first ③ and nintedanib three weeks later ④ we witnessed an immediate clinical improvement and a prompt, continuous decrease in serum ferritin levels to 304 μg/L, which allowed to taper prednisone in short, 10-days intervals. An initial decline of FVC from 59% to 37% was followed by a modest recovery to 50% of predicted value (y-axis right; dotted line). Details of doses of the medications used, including the tapering scheme of the corticosteroid, are found in the main text.
